title: Why democracy will never work
content:
🌿 🧠 Topic Overview

  • Democracy might be mathematically impossible due to irrational voting methods.
  • The "first past the post" system is commonly used but can lead to outcomes where the majority does not elect the winning candidate.
  • In the last century, only 2 out of 21 instances saw the majority vote for the party that held power in the British Parliament.
  • The "spoiler effect" occurs when similar candidates split votes, as seen in the 2000 US presidential election with Ralph Nader.
  • First past the post incentivizes strategic voting, often resulting in a two-party system due to Duverger's Law.
  • Alternatives like ranked-choice voting (instant runoff) can mitigate some issues but have their own complications, such as potential paradoxes.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • First Past the Post: A voting system where the candidate with the most votes wins, regardless of majority.
  • Spoiler Effect: When a candidate draws votes away from a similar candidate, affecting the election outcome.
  • Duverger's Law: A principle stating that single-winner electoral systems tend to favor a two-party system.
  • Instant Runoff Voting: A method where voters rank candidates, and the least popular candidates are eliminated until one achieves a majority.
  • Condorcet's Paradox: A situation where collective preferences can cycle, leading to no clear winner.
  • Arrow's Impossibility Theorem: A theorem stating that no ranked voting system can satisfy all fairness criteria with three or more candidates.

🧬 Processes / Mechanisms

  1. First Past the Post Voting: Voters select one candidate; the one with the most votes wins.
  2. Ranked-Choice Voting: Voters rank candidates; if no majority, the least popular is eliminated, and votes are redistributed until a majority is found.

📊 Comparisons & Tables

Term Definition

Ranked-Choice Voting Voters rank candidates; eliminates the least popular until a majority is reached.

First Past the Post Can lead to a party winning without majority support 21 instances in British Parliament where majority did not vote for the winning party

💡 Applications / Examples

  • The 2000 US presidential election illustrates the spoiler effect with Ralph Nader's candidacy.
  • Ranked-choice voting can lead to more civil campaigns, as seen in the Minneapolis mayoral race.

✍️ Mini-Quiz (3 quick checks)

  • Q: What is the main flaw of the first past the post system?
  • Answer: It can result in a candidate winning without majority support.
  • Q: What does Duverger's Law state?
  • Answer: It states that single-winner electoral systems tend to favor a two-party system.
  • Q: What is Arrow's Impossibility Theorem?
  • Answer: It states that no ranked voting system can satisfy all fairness criteria with three or more candidates.
